title: ROMANS 1 SAYS WOMEN EXCHANGED “NATURAL RELATIONS”—BUT WHAT ARGUMENT IS PAUL ACTUALLY MAKING?
paragraphs: ROMANS 1 SAYS WOMEN EXCHANGED “NATURAL RELATIONS”—BUT WHAT ARGUMENT IS PAUL ACTUALLY MAKING?
Romans 1:26 Is About Sexual Sin—But If That Is All You See, You Have Missed Something Terrifying About Paul’s Warning
There is a sentence in Romans that people quote in arguments, whisper in uncomfortable conversations, throw across comment sections, and sometimes use like a weapon.
But Paul did not write it as a weapon for respectable sinners to use against people whose sins make them uncomfortable.
He wrote it in the middle of an indictment of the human race.
And if you read Romans 1:26 carefully enough, something unsettling happens.
You eventually realize Paul is not merely talking about “those people.”
He is talking about what happens to human beings when we exchange God for something else.
And sooner or later, that means he is talking about you.
About me.
About all of us.
Here is the line.
In the Greek text of Romans 1:26 we read:
“Διὰ τοῦτο παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ θεὸς εἰς πάθη ἀτιμίας· αἵ τε γὰρ θήλειαι αὐτῶν μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν.”
A close rendering is:
“For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions; for their females exchanged the natural use for that which is contrary to nature.”
The wording matters.
Paul uses μετήλλαξαν — metēllaxan.
They “exchanged.”
He uses φυσικὴν — physikēn, meaning natural or according to nature.
He speaks of χρῆσιν — chrēsin, “use” or “relations,” a word functioning sexually in this context.
And then comes the phrase that has generated centuries of discussion:
παρὰ φύσιν — para physin.
“Contrary to nature.”

The Greek wording itself is not mysterious. The debate concerns what Paul means by it and how his argument functions within Romans as a whole. The immediate context makes clear that sexual relations are in view, and verse 27 removes much of the ambiguity because Paul immediately parallels the women with males abandoning sexual relations with females and desiring other males.
So we should not make the text say less than it says.
But neither should we make it say something Paul never said.

Paul does not discuss modern psychological categories of sexual orientation in this passage. He does not pause to distinguish every possible circumstance, biography, temptation, relationship, or contemporary identity category.
His language concerns actions within a much larger theological argument.
And that argument begins before Romans 1:26.
That is where things become uncomfortable.
Because before Paul speaks about exchanging sexual relations, he speaks about another exchange.
Romans 1:23 says humanity “exchanged the glory of the immortal God” for created images.
Then Romans 1:25 says they “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” and worshiped creation rather than the Creator.
Then Romans 1:26 uses exchange language again.
Do you see the pattern?
Glory exchanged.
Truth exchanged.
Natural relations exchanged.

Paul is describing disordered human existence flowing from disordered worship. Romans 1:18–32 repeatedly connects humanity’s refusal to honor the Creator with the corruption that follows when created things occupy the Creator’s place.
That means Romans 1 is not fundamentally a chapter about homosexual behavior with a few introductory verses about God.
It is an indictment of idolatry and human rebellion, within which Paul presents same-sex sexual behavior as one manifestation of humanity’s disorder after exchanging the Creator for creation.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because if you read Romans 1:26 and your first response is,
“Finally. A verse about them.”
Keep reading.
Paul is coming for your idols too.
Maybe yours does not involve sexuality.
Maybe your idol wears a suit.
Maybe it lives in your bank account.
Maybe it sleeps beside you.
Maybe people applaud yours.
Maybe yours stands behind a pulpit.
Maybe yours is your reputation.
Your career.
Your body.
Your politics.
Your relationship.
Your ministry.
Your anger.
Your need to be admired.
Your secret pornography.
Your heterosexual lust.
Your bitterness.
Your obsession with money.
Your religious pride.
Your carefully constructed Christian image.
Anything created can become spiritually catastrophic when it receives the trust, obedience, identity, devotion, or worship belonging ultimately to the Creator.
And that is the deeper horror of Romans 1.
Sin does not merely make us break rules.
Sin rearranges worship.
We exchange.
God for pleasure.
Truth for convenience.
Holiness for appetite.
Obedience for autonomy.
The Creator for creation.
And eventually we can become so accustomed to the exchange that what once disturbed our conscience begins to feel normal.
Then comes perhaps one of the most frightening expressions in Romans 1:
παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός — paredōken autous ho Theos.
“God gave them over.”
Paul repeats this idea three times—Romans 1:24, 1:26, and 1:28.
God gave them over.
God gave them over.
God gave them over.
Sometimes judgment does not look like lightning falling from heaven.
Sometimes judgment looks like God allowing rebellious humanity to travel farther down the road it demanded.
That should terrify every one of us.
There is a frightening possibility in sin: eventually the person saying, “God, leave me alone,” may experience something resembling the very thing requested.
Yet Romans does not end there.
Thank God.
Because Paul is building an argument larger than Romans 1.
And before the religious reader can become comfortable while watching “those sinners” condemned, Romans 2 turns the spotlight.
“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges…”
The trap closes.
The person nodding through Romans 1 suddenly finds himself standing in the courtroom.
Then Paul keeps going until Romans 3 delivers the verdict no self-righteous human being wanted:
All have sinned.
All fall short of the glory of God.
Not all people commit identical sins.
Scripture never requires us to pretend every behavior is morally identical.
But every human being desperately needs the righteousness he cannot manufacture for himself.
That is where Jesus Christ stops being an accessory to this conversation.
He becomes the only hope in it.
Romans 1 cannot faithfully be preached as, “Look how disgusting those people are.”
The trajectory of Romans is:
Look what sin has done to us.
Look how desperately we need righteousness.
And then look at what God has done in Jesus Christ.
This is why Christians must resist two opposite temptations.
One temptation says love requires us to edit Scripture until nobody is confronted.
It does not.
Jesus did not die because sin was imaginary.
Grace is breathtaking precisely because our guilt is real.
The other temptation says faithfulness requires Christians to speak biblical truth without tenderness, humility, tears, patience, or awareness of their own desperate dependence upon grace.
It does not.
You can defend a true doctrine with a Pharisee’s heart.
You can correctly identify another person’s sin while remaining astonishingly blind to your own.
Romans 1 gives us no permission to rewrite what Paul calls sin.
Romans 2 gives us no permission to become arrogant about somebody else’s sin.
Romans 3 gives us no permission to imagine ourselves righteous enough to save ourselves.
And the Gospel gives us no permission to believe any repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
That includes the sexually broken.
The sexually confused.
The sexually immoral.
The adulterer.
The fornicator.
The pornography addict.
The person experiencing same-sex attraction.
The proud church member.
The greedy businessman.
The gossip.
The bitter spouse.
The hypocrite.
The person who has hidden an entire second life behind a Christian profile picture.
Jesus did not come looking for people who could prove they had never been dirty.
He came to save sinners.
This does not mean every desire suddenly disappears when someone comes to Christ.
Christian discipleship has never meant, “I encountered Jesus, therefore temptation ceased to exist.”
Sometimes obedience means carrying a cross through desires that continue screaming.
Sometimes holiness means telling your body no because you have told Jesus yes.
And that principle does not belong uniquely to Christians experiencing same-sex attraction.
Every disciple eventually encounters desires that cannot be permitted to become lord.
The question underneath Christian sexuality is therefore much larger than:
“What do I feel?”
The deeper question is:
Who is Lord?
If Jesus is Lord, my desires do not possess final authority.
Neither do yours.
Our bodies belong to Christ.
Our sexuality belongs to Christ.
Our relationships belong to Christ.
Our loneliness belongs to Christ.
Our wounds belong to Christ.
Our identity belongs to Christ.
Even the parts of ourselves we desperately wish God would leave untouched belong to Christ.
That is where repentance becomes beautiful instead of merely frightening.
Repentance is not God standing at the door saying, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will love you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Christ came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose for sinners.
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Christ forgives sinners.
Christ begins transforming sinners.
Grace does not tell you that your chains were actually jewelry.
Grace breaks chains.
Grace does not rename darkness so we can comfortably remain inside it.
Grace brings us into the light.
And grace does not mean Jesus looks at our sin and shrugs.
Grace means Jesus looked at sinners with a love so staggering that He went to the cross.
That is why Romans 1:26 should never become ammunition for cruelty.
If someone reading this experiences same-sex attraction, you are not a theological specimen.
You are a human being.
You should not be mocked.
You should not be treated as though temptation itself places you beyond the possibility of Christian fellowship.
You should not be reduced to one dimension of your experience.
And you should never be told that Jesus has no place for you.
Come to Christ.
Not because Christians are better than you.
We are not.
Come because Christ is better than every master that promises freedom while demanding your soul.
And if you are heterosexual, do not breathe a sigh of relief.
Paul has not given you permission to leave the courtroom.
You can affirm biblical marriage and still worship money.
You can condemn homosexual behavior while secretly consuming pornography.
You can defend “family values” while emotionally destroying your family.

You can quote Romans 1 while ignoring your greed, envy, deceit, gossip, arrogance, disobedience, faithlessness, ruthlessness, and lack of mercy—the very kinds of sins Paul continues listing before the chapter ends.
Perhaps that is why Romans 1 feels so different when we stop reading it as ammunition.
The chapter becomes a mirror.
And mirrors are dangerous when we have spent years learning how to look at everybody except ourselves.
Maybe this article found you while you are hiding something.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your church friends think you are strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe your browser history tells another story.
Maybe your relationship tells another story.
Maybe your private desires tell another story.
Maybe you have spent years defending Scripture publicly while negotiating with sin privately.
Maybe you are tired.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of performing.
Tired of promising God, “Never again,” only to find yourself standing in the same ruins.
Hear this carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus is not intimidated by serious sinners.
The cross was built for guilty people.
You do not need another excuse.
You need a Savior.
You do not need someone to tell you darkness is light.
You need Someone powerful enough to bring you out of darkness.
His name is Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
Not the polished version.
Not your church version.
Not your Facebook version.
The truth.
“Jesus, this is what I have become.”
“Jesus, this is what I desire.”
“Jesus, this is what I have done.”
“Jesus, this is what I cannot seem to defeat.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That prayer is not the end of discipleship.
It may be where honesty finally begins.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk into the light.
Find mature believers who will tell you the truth without treating you like garbage.
Submit your desires to Christ.
Open Scripture even when Scripture confronts you.
Pray when you feel nothing.
Obey when obedience hurts.
Get up when you fall.
Confess instead of hiding.
And remember that sanctification is not you convincing Jesus to keep loving you by becoming impressive.
It is the lifelong work of God conforming redeemed people to the image of His Son.
So what argument is Paul making when he says women exchanged natural relations for those “contrary to nature”?

At the immediate level, Paul is speaking about sexual conduct, and verse 27 confirms the same-sex dimension of the discussion. The wording should not be erased merely because modern readers find it difficult. Serious scholarly defenses of the traditional reading likewise understand παρὰ φύσιν here in relation to created order rather than merely an individual’s personal preference or a passing social convention.
But Paul’s theological argument is larger than one sexual act.

Romans 1 portrays humanity exchanging the Creator for creation and then experiencing disorder flowing from that fundamental rebellion. Romans 2 confronts the judging moralist. Romans 3 gathers humanity under sin and unveils our need for God’s righteousness.
So if you use Romans 1 only to win an argument about homosexuality, you may win the argument and miss Paul’s devastating point.
The ultimate human catastrophe is not merely that people desire wrongly.
It is that humanity has worshiped wrongly.
And the ultimate Christian answer is therefore not heterosexuality.
It is not conservative respectability.
It is not winning a culture war.
It is not pretending temptation does not exist.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ forgiving.
Christ transforming.
Christ calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture outrage.
Not to build a community where religious people congratulate themselves for being better than everybody else.
But to keep pointing wounded, struggling, compromised, searching human beings toward Scripture and ultimately toward Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail of your private life.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would own you forever, tell your testimony if you can.
Somebody silently reading the comments may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
Send it to the person who thinks Christians have nothing to offer except condemnation.
Send it to the churchgoer who knows everybody else’s sins but has stopped examining his own heart.
One day you may need to read it again when the temptation is yours.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the person who does not believe any of this yet.
Because somewhere tonight there is a person staring at a screen while losing a war nobody knows they are fighting.
Maybe they will never tell you.
Maybe they have learned to smile while dying inside.
Maybe they believe what they have done has already written the final chapter of their life.
That is why we keep telling this story.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
But grace is real too.
The cross is real.
The empty tomb is real.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is real.
And Jesus Christ is still receiving sinners.
Romans 1 tells the truth about what happens when humanity exchanges God.
The Gospel tells the breathtaking truth about the God who came searching for rebels anyway.
You may have exchanged truth for a lie.
You may have exchanged holiness for pleasure.
You may have exchanged years of your life for something that promised freedom and left you chained.
But if you are still breathing, your scandal does not have to write your final sentence.
Bring Jesus the chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read—and watch what the Author of grace can do with a story you thought was already over.
